series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 1/4] block: do not issue background swap bios as root
series_items.patch_summary: This RFC patch proposes to modify the behavior of bio_issue_as_root_blkg() to not issue background swap bios as root, allowing cgroup IO controllers to throttle such I/O. The change is motivated by the fact that some swap writes are best effort and can be throttled without stalling indefinitely on swap writes.

review_comments.author: Christoph Hellwig
review_comments.summary: Questioned whether REQ_BACKGROUND implies that I/O can be throttled, suggesting that the caller should tolerate a failure if it is foreground paging.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Mon, Sep 28, 2026 at 10:18:36AM +0200, Alexandre Ghiti wrote:
> bio_issue_as_root_blkg() issues every REQ_SWAP bio as root, bypassing
> the cgroup IO controllers, because reclaim cannot stall indefinitely on
> swap writes. Some swap writes are not urgent though: zswap writeback is
> best effort.
> 
> Such a bio cannot simply drop REQ_SWAP: dm-crypt and dm-thin rely on it
> for limit_swap_bios, which caps in-flight swap bios to avoid a memory
> deadlock, see commit a666e5c05e7c ("dm: fix deadlock when swapping to
> encrypted device").

Is that true?  REQ_BACKGROUND very much implies the I/O can the throttled
and thus better not be foreground paging, and thus the caller should be
able to tolerate a failure.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 2/4] mm/zswap: turn shrink_memcg_cb()'s argument into a flags word
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the `shrink_memcg_cb()` function in the zswap module to accept a flags word instead of a boolean pointer as an argument. The flags word allows callers to pass additional information, specifically whether the walk stopped at an entry already in the swap cache. This change does not introduce any functional changes but rather provides a more flexible way for callers to interact with the function. The patch defines a new flag `ZSWAP_SHRINK_SWAPCACHE` and updates the function's logic accordingly.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 3/4] mm/zswap: allow writeback to be throttled by the cgroup IO controllers
series_items.patch_summary: This patch allows the cgroup IO controllers to throttle zswap writeback operations by introducing a new 'throttled' flag in the swap_io_ctx structure. When this flag is set, the write operation is issued as background I/O instead of being exempt from cgroup throttling, which avoids priority inversion and ensures that memory reclaim is not stalled for other workloads.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 4/4] mm/zswap: move reclaim-driven writeback to a kworker
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the reclaim-driven writeback of zswap to a kworker, improving performance by avoiding stalls in application threads or kswapd. The kworker writes back swap entries in batches of SWAP_CLUSTER_MAX while holding a reference on the memcg, and reports nothing freed until the worker runs. This change is necessary because cgroup IO controllers throttle zswap writeback, causing stalls that were observed in production workloads.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This RFC patch series aims to improve the performance of zswap by making its shrinker writeback work with iocost. The current implementation causes a large production workload to be slower when zswap is enabled, due to two main issues: (1) zswap writeback being charged as debt and causing stalls in application allocations, and (2) throttled writes sleeping in their submitter, which can be an application thread. The patches propose to throttle zswap writeback instead of making it REQ_SWAP, and move the reclaim-driven writeback to a per-lruvec kworker.

version_history.subject: [PATCH 2/2] btrfs: commit after deleting an unused block group if system space is low

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch addresses a problem where deleting multiple unused block groups in one transaction can fail due to insufficient system space, resulting in an -ENOSPC error. To solve this issue, the patch introduces a mechanism that checks for low system space and commits a single transaction to delete a single block group at a time. This approach allows the system to recover unallocated space and improves the chances of successfully allocating system chunks. The patch modifies the btrfs_delete_unused_bgs function in fs/btrfs/block-group.c to implement this new behavior.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH 1/2] btrfs: allocate additional SYSTEM space earlier

version_history.subject: [PATCH 1/2] btrfs: allocate additional SYSTEM space earlier

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch addresses a performance issue in Btrfs file systems where large block devices can accumulate thousands of system chunks, leading to slow deletion of unused block groups when the file system is filled up and then freed en-masse. The problem arises because the current implementation allocates new system chunks only when the space left is smaller than the reservation for a single chunk tree update. To fix this, the patch introduces a new function `system_space_needed` that estimates the upper bound on bytes needed to modify every leaf in the chunk tree and allocates additional system space earlier, ensuring that all block groups can be deleted in one transaction.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 1/3] mm/huge_memory: make thp_underused() work for mTHP folios
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the thp_underused() function to make it work with mTHP folios, which are larger than PMD-sized folios. The function is made size-aware instead of hardcoded to PMD-sized folios. A new helper function, thp_can_be_underused(), is introduced to check if a folio can be underused based on the number of zero-filled pages and the sysctl maximum value. This change will allow anonymous mTHP folios to be added to the deferred split list in future patches.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 2/3] mm/huge_memory: don't queue folios that can never be underused
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the handling of anonymous PMD-sized folios in the Linux kernel by skipping the queuing of folios that can never be underused, reducing unnecessary work and improving performance. The default khugepaged/max_ptes_none setting causes the shrinker to never split these folios for being underused, so they are not queued. This change is particularly important for a subsequent patch that adds anonymous mTHP folios to the deferred split list, as it prevents small mTHP orders from taking the list_lru lock on every anonymous fault.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 3/3] mm/memory: add anonymous mTHP folios to the deferred split list
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds anonymous mTHP (huge page) folios to the deferred split list in the Linux kernel's memory management code. This allows for underused splitting of huge pages, which can help reclaim unused parts of large memory allocations when the system is under memory pressure. The patch addresses a problem where fully mapped huge pages that are mostly zero-filled do not get split by the deferred split shrinker, leading to memory regressions. The solution involves mirroring the behavior for PMD-sized folios and adding a check to minimize overhead on common fault paths.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series addresses memory regressions caused by enabling 2M THP=always on arm64 with 64k base pages. The patches split underused anonymous mTHP folios, which are not currently reclaimed under memory pressure. Patch 1 makes the thp_underused() function size-aware to accommodate larger folio sizes. Patch 2 optimizes existing behavior by keeping folios that can never be found underused off the deferred split queue. Patch 3 queues anonymous mTHP folios from map_anon_folio_pte_nopf(), mirroring what is already done for PMD folios. The patches aim to provide a solution for deploying 2M THP=always on arm64 without causing memory regressions.

review_comments.author: Lance Yang
review_comments.summary: Lance Yang noted that the use of an absolute value for khugepaged_max_ptes_none as both the mTHP underused threshold and the PMD collapse threshold is inconsistent, leading to different values being used depending on whether it's applied in mTHP or PMD context. He suggested using a per-order value instead, which would also allow preserving the current behavior by leaving max_ptes_none unset.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Wed, Sep 16, 2026 at 03:44:34PM -0700, Joanne Koong wrote:
>PMD-sized THPs that are mostly zero-filled are reclaimed under memory
>pressure by the deferred split shrinker, but this is not done for mTHP
>folios. At Meta we would like to deploy 2M THP=always on arm64 with 64k
>base pages, as 2M provides the contpte benefits while the PMD size there
>(512M) is too big to use. However, 2M THP=always causes memory regressions
>unless the unused portions of those folios can be broken down and
>reclaimed.
>
>v1 did two things. It scaled khugepaged_max_ptes_none down per folio order and
>it queued every anonymous mTHP folio. David objected to the scaling since
>collapse had already rejected proportional scaling as either letting the memory
>footprint creep or being confusing to reason about. David and Barry separately
>objected to the queuing, which adds list_lru lock contention on every anonymous
>fault, and hurts lower-order use cases such as Android's order-2-only
>configuration. Johannes suggested keeping khugepaged_max_ptes_none absolute and
>simply not queuing folios that could never exceed it, which addresses both.
>
>Read as an absolute count, khugepaged_max_ptes_none also implies the
>smallest folio that takes part in underused splitting. A 2M folio on 64k
>base pages is 32 pages, so the knob has to be set below 32 for those to
>be queued at all, and any folio with no more pages than the value stays off
>the queue entirely.

Em ... I'm not sure max_ptes_none should also become the mTHP underused
threshold ...

Say we're on arm64 with 64K pages and set it to 16. Khugepaged PMD
collapse uses 16, while mTHP collapse turns the same value into 0. With
this series, an order-5 (2 MiB) mTHP enters the deferred split queue
because it has 32 pages, and is considered underused once more than 16
pages are zero-filled. So the same knob means 16, 0, and 16 depending on
where it is used ... That's a bit odd ... no?

Would a per-order value make more sense here?

An unset value could preserve the current behavior, while an explicit
value could control both mTHP collapse and underused splitting. That
would also give us a way to leave max_ptes_none as the legacy fallback
instead of adding more meaning to it :)

Cheers, Lance

>Patch 1 makes thp_underused() folio-size aware. Today it only ever sees
>PMD-sized folios, so it assumes HPAGE_PMD_NR pages throughout. Patch 3

>when the region is almost fully populated. That is fine for the deployment

>

Author: Nico Pache <nico.pache@linux.dev>
Date:   Fri Jun 5 10:14:11 2026 -0600

    mm/khugepaged: generalize __collapse_huge_page_* for mTHP support

    generalize the order of the __collapse_huge_page_* and collapse_max_*
    functions to support future mTHP collapse.

    The current mechanism for determining collapse with the
    khugepaged_max_ptes_none value is not designed with mTHP in mind.  This
    raises a key design issue: if we support user defined max_pte_none values
    (even those scaled by order), a collapse of a lower order can introduces
    an feedback loop, or "creep", when max_ptes_none is set to a value greater
    than HPAGE_PMD_NR / 2.  [1]

    With this configuration, a successful collapse to order N will populate
    enough pages to satisfy the collapse condition on order N+1 on the next
    scan.  This leads to unnecessary work and memory churn.

    collapse support to two max_ptes_none values, 0 and HPAGE_PMD_NR - 1.

      available mTHP order.

    any non-supported max_ptes_none value is configured with mTHP enabled.

    khugepaged_max_ptes_swap parameters, and will fail if it encounters a

all contend on one lruvec, running 80 threads x 16 MB x 200 loops.

running perf lock contention on folio_lruvec_lock_irqsave ("lock wait"
is all 80 threads summed):

    size                 contentions   lock wait   folios/MB

    mTHP-16K          4203612      392.8 s        64
    mTHP-32K          2064073      190.5 s        32
    mTHP-64K           212012        1.7 s          16
    mTHP-128K          117993        1.8 s           8
    mTHP-256K           64532        4.2 s           4
    mTHP-512K           32485        3.1 s           2
    mTHP-1024K           4313        0.3 s           1
    mTHP-2048K            725        0.1 s           0.5

mTHP-16k results in more lock contentions (though I didn't see a
runtime regression. I saw that 16k comes out a bit faster than 4k in
wall time), but 64k results in significantly less. For mTHP-32k, I see
less time overall spent waiting, but 2x the lock contention.

I re-ran the benchmark with the 3 patches in this series applied, with
the khugepaged/max_ptes_none sysfs value set to 0 so every folio gets
queued (the worst case) and measured the queueing cost by switching
shrink_underused on/off. I saw:

      size                 runtime delta between on/off   folios/MB
      mTHP-16K             +15.8%                                64
      mTHP-32K             +11.5%                                32
      mTHP-64K              +1.1%                                16
      mTHP-128K             +1.2%                                 8
      mTHP-256K             -0.6%                                  4
      mTHP-512K             +0.5%                                 2
      mTHP-1024K            -1.2%                                 1
      mTHP-2048K            -0.3%                              0.5

which mirrors the same pattern/trend as above (eg regresses at the 16k
and 32k cases, but not for 64k+).

I ran a perf analysis and the delta doesn't come from the deferred
split list's own lock, but actually from folio_lruvec_lock_irqsave:

      shrink_underused             0            1
      runtime                     6.00s           6.86s           +14.3%
      lruvec contentions     4206376      4234324      +0.7%
      lruvec wait            406.4 s           485.8 s         +19.5%
      avg wait                96.5us           114.5us
      list_lru_lock           absent            absent

The lruvec contentions count doesn't move much (0.7%) but the time
spent waiting goes up 19.5%. I think that's coming from the free path
rather than the fault path. In folios_put_refs(),
__page_cache_release() keeps the lruvec locked across the whole batch,
and from what I'm seeing, folio_unqueue_deferred_split() gets called
from inside that loop. I don't think your lru cache series helps this
directly since it batches on the add side but this cost is coming from
the free side inside a section that's already batched, but I think it
should help indirectly, since there would be less lruvec pressure /
contention overall. I'm not 100% sure about this, but think it might
be possible to move the unqueue from the deferred list to outside the
lruvec lock hold, though I need to look more into this.

For now though, I think it makes sense to have a hard-coded minimum
folio size for the underused shrinker, as you and David suggested.
Based on the results above, I think having 64k as the cut-off makes
sense.

Agreed. And if/when collapse gains proportional support later on,
having split already scaled means one value governing both instead of
two.

Agreed.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 RESEND 1/5] mm/memcontrol: flatten try_charge_memcg control flow
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the try_charge_memcg function in the Linux kernel's memory control module to simplify its control flow by separating the logic for memsw and memory page counters into distinct paths.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 RESEND 2/5] mm/page_counter: introduce per-CPU stock
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a per-CPU stock representation in the page_counter layer, mirroring the existing implementation in memcg. The new struct page_counter_stock_pcp preserves the functionality of its memcg counterpart and adds a backpointer to the base of the percpu stock. The patch also updates the page_counter structure to include pointers to the percpu stock and cgroup_subsys_state. No functional changes are intended, but rather a copy of existing code from memcg.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 RESEND 3/5] mm/page_counter: make page_counter_try_charge() stock-aware
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the page_counter_try_charge() function to be stock-aware, allowing it to consume stock transparently while preserving the same semantics as try_charge_memcg's greedy charge attempt and refill behavior. The function now takes two new parameters: may_batch, which preserves the behavior of !allow_spinning scenarios, and nr_charged, which reflects the size of the successful hierarchy charge. This change is intended to improve memory.high accounting for current->memcg_nr_pages_over_high without affecting existing functionality.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 RESEND 4/5] mm/memcontrol: move memory stock to page counters
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the memory stock from memcg to page counters, allowing for more flexibility in managing memory usage. The transition is done while preserving the legacy user-visible memory <= memory+swap invariant. The patch also removes unused memcg code and prepares for future work on introducing additional page counters without affecting cgroup v2 users.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 RESEND 5/5] mm/memcontrol: add stock to the memsw page counter
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a separate stock (bank) to the memsw page counter in Linux's memory control system, allowing it to operate independently of the main memory bank. The patch introduces new functions for scheduling and draining the stock, ensuring that failed allocations do not replenish the newly attached memsw stock. It also preserves user-visible cgroup-v1 invariant by reporting memory.memsw.usage_in_bytes as the larger raw value.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch moves the stock abstraction from mem_cgroup to page_counter, allowing each page_counter to have its own per-CPU cache of pre-charged pages. This change is intended to improve performance and scalability for future work on multiple page_counters in a single memcg. The existing seven-slot per-CPU design and drain policy are retained. For memcg v1 users, this decouples the memory and memsw stocks, potentially leading to different sizes of precharged cache for each. To maintain an invariant between these two stocks, the patch reports the larger value of usage_in_bytes for memsw reporting.

series_items.patch_summary: This patch removes an unnecessary mmgrab() reference in the madvise_collapse() function, which is already holding a valid mm_users reference. The redundant mmgrab() call is dropped to simplify the code and avoid potential issues.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 02/13] mm/khugepaged: count collapses where khugepaged makes them
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the khugepaged functionality to count collapses where it makes them, rather than relying on the caller to increment a shared counter. The daemon can now keep its own counter without needing to test who called the collapse function. This change simplifies the code and improves maintainability.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 03/13] mm/khugepaged: rename mthp_present_ptes bitmap to eligible_ptes
series_items.patch_summary: This patch renames the bitmap 'mthp_present_ptes' in the mm/khugepaged module to 'eligible_ptes'. The name change reflects that a set bit in this bitmap indicates not only that a PTE is present, but also that it has passed various checks. This change does not introduce any functional changes and is intended to improve clarity of the code.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 04/13] mm/collapse: add collapse.h for the collapse interface
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new header file, mm/collapse.h, to separate the interface and implementation of the collapse feature from the khugepaged.c file. The collapse feature is used for page migration and memory compaction. The new header file defines an enum for scan results and a struct for control parameters, as well as two constants related to page table entries. This separation improves code organization and maintainability.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 05/13] mm/collapse: state what a collapse may do in the policy
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new struct called collapse_policy to store the policy decisions made by the caller before asking for a collapse. The policy includes limits on missing, swapped-out or shared PTEs in a window, as well as other settings such as whether to look at used ranges and how to handle MADV_FREE'd pages. The patch replaces scattered tests throughout the collapse path with reads from the collapse_policy struct, simplifying the code and removing the need for khugepaged to look up who called it. The policy is filled once per scan pass by khugepaged and once per call by MADV_COLLAPSE.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 11/13] mm/collapse: work out the orders a VMA allows once per VMA
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the way the kernel handles memory collapsing by allowing it to work out the allowed orders for a VMA only once per VMA, rather than once per PTE table. This is done by passing the mask of allowed orders from collapse_possible_orders() directly to the functions that need it, and sampling it once per VMA instead of once per table. review_comments.summary: Author addressed a concern about the collapse engine and its callers being intertwined, proposing to separate them by introducing an interface and splitting the call in two with the lock as the boundary.
review_comments.raw_body:
From: "Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta)" <kas@kernel.org>

[ This is the first of the cleanups I said I would front-load ]

There is no line between the collapse engine and the callers that ask for
a collapse.  khugepaged.c holds both, and they reach into each other.

 - Sixteen tests through the collapse path read cc->is_khugepaged to work
   out what they are allowed to do, when every one of those decisions was
   made by the caller before it asked.

 - collapse_single_pmd() does both halves of a collapse behind one call and
   drops mmap_lock somewhere in the middle.  Which of its paths dropped it
   is not something a caller can see, so it hands back a bool and the
   caller keeps track.

 - MADV_COLLAPSE's implementation -- the walk over the user's range, the
   per-PMD loop, the errno translation -- sits in khugepaged.c, which is
   the daemon's file.

So: draw the line.  State what a caller allows in a policy, split the call
in two with the lock as the boundary, and move the syscall to madvise.c.
What the engine offers is then three calls, with the lock state written
down against each, and a policy the caller fills for itself:

    collapse_control_init(cc)         once, before the first table
    collapse_policy_*(&cc->policy)    what this caller allows
    collapse_scan_pmd(vma, addr, ...) per table, under mmap_lock
    collapse_run_pmd(mm, addr, ...)   when a scan found work, no mmap_lock

The engine stays in khugepaged.c for now; what changes is that it has an
interface, and that neither half has to ask about the other.  madvise.c
gains the operation it should have had all along.

Changes since v3
================

  https://lore.kernel.org/all/20260916093145.4022188-1-kirill@shutemov.name/

 - Patch 5: the PTE limits come as two sets, struct collapse_limits for a
   PMD-sized window and one for anything smaller, and the strict_sub_pmd
   flag goes.  The warning for a max_ptes_none between 0 and the maximum
   moves to where khugepaged fills its policy.  The fields only one side
   reads are prefixed anon_ or file_.  collapse_policy_forced() is
   collapse_policy_madvise() (David).

 - Patch 8 is new: collapse_file() is called from collapse_single_pmd()
   rather than from inside collapse_scan_file(), so the file scan stops at
   the decision before the scan/run split.  The writeback retry and the
   tracepoint change move into it, so patch 9 is only the split (David).

 - Patch 9: no collapse_control_release().  It had nothing to release in
   this series; it comes back with the engine, where init allocates.  The
   check that the last scan was run stays at the top of collapse_scan_pmd()
   (David).

 - Patch 10: the changelog says why the lock boundary belongs to the
   caller (David).

 - Patch 11: both callers pass their TVA type as the literal it is rather
   than reading it back from the policy (David).

 - Patch 12: kerneldoc on every function collapse.h declares (David).

 - Acked-by from David Hildenbrand on 1-4, 6 and 7; Reviewed-by from
   Baolin Wang on 10.  Reviewed-by dropped from 5 and 9, which changed.

Changes since v2
================

  https://lore.kernel.org/all/20260910120238.2529819-1-kirill@shutemov.name/

 - Patch 8: the file scan returns SCAN_PTE_MAPPED_HUGEPAGE as it is and
   the run is handed what the scan returned, so it goes straight to
   retracting the PTE table when it sees it.  The scan_retract_only flag
   and the result round trip go, and the two copies of the file put become
   one helper (Zi).  Patches 9-12 follow the new signature.

 - Patch 8: mthp_collapse() and collapse_huge_page() read the orders and
   the referenced and swapped-out counts from collapse_control instead of
   taking them as arguments (Baolin).

 - Patch 11: each interface function is documented where it is defined,
   with the lock state on entry and exit.  The overview in collapse.h
   stays (Zi).

 - Reviewed-by from Zi Yan on 8 and 9, and from Zi Yan and Baolin Wang
   on 5 and 10.

Changes since v1
================

  https://lore.kernel.org/all/cover.1788533997.git.kas@kernel.org/

 - Rebased onto mm-new with Vernon Yang's tracepoint fixes in it.  Patch 8
   no longer merges the two calls to each scan tracepoint, since the base
   already has one; its changelog now says what the status field reports.

 - Patch 3: nr_occupied_ptes is nr_eligible_ptes, and the mthp_collapse()
   comment counts eligible PTEs too (Zi, Baolin).

 - Patch 4: no comments on the two constants (Baolin).

 - Patch 5: one line per policy field (Baolin).

 - Patch 8: the file side is split like the anonymous one (Zi).
   collapse_scan_file() runs under mmap_lock in the scan and only reads;
   collapse_file() runs in the run.  See Behaviour below.

 - Reviewed-by from Zi Yan and Baolin Wang on 1-4, 6 and 7.

Patches
=======

The first three stand alone and can be taken separately:

  1  drop the mmgrab() MADV_COLLAPSE has held since 7d8faaf15545
  2  count collapses in khugepaged's own walk, where the daemon's
     bookkeeping belongs
  3  rename cc->mthp_present_ptes to eligible_ptes, which is what a set
     bit means

Then the interface, in order:

  4  add collapse.h, and move enum scan_result, struct collapse_control
     and the two constants into it
  5  struct collapse_policy, filled by the caller; the is_khugepaged
     tests become field reads, and the flag goes
  6  drop collapse_possible(), a wrapper that only turns a mask into a bool
  7  collapse_control_init_scan() is a per-table reset, so name it
     collapse_scan_reset()
  8  call collapse_file() from collapse_single_pmd(), so the file scan
     stops at the decision
  9  give the scan and the collapse a function each: collapse_scan_pmd()
     and collapse_run_pmd()
 10  open-code the entry point that joined them, so each caller owns the
     lock across the boundary and the bool goes
 11  work out the orders a VMA allows once per VMA, not once per table
 12  declare the three calls in collapse.h, with the lock rules
 13  MADV_COLLAPSE moves to madvise.c

Behaviour
=========

No functional change is intended.  Nothing here changes which tables get
collapsed, into what, or what MADV_COLLAPSE returns.  The tracepoints are
the one place a change can be seen from outside; the rest is where work
happens, not what it does.

 - Patches 8 and 9: mm_khugepaged_scan_file and mm_khugepaged_scan_pmd
   fire before the collapse rather than after it.  For an accepted table
   their status field reads SCAN_SUCCEED, where it used to carry what the
   collapse made of the table; that is now for mm_khugepaged_collapse_file
   and mm_collapse_huge_page to report.

Four things move that a reader should not have to find in the diff:

 - Patch 5: khugepaged fills its policy once per scan pass, so the
   max_ptes_* limits and the defrag setting behind the allocation mask are
   sampled once per pass rather than once per table.  A knob written
   mid-pass takes effect on the next pass instead of the next table.

 - Patch 8: the writeback retry re-runs collapse_file() alone, where it
   used to rescan the page cache first.

 - Patch 9: the file scan runs under mmap_lock, where before the lock was
   given up first.  A file table the scan refuses no longer costs
   khugepaged an unlock, a trip back through khugepaged_do_scan(), a
   relock and a VMA lookup; only a table it goes on to collapse does.

 - Patch 11: which orders a table is scanned for is sampled once per VMA
   rather than once per table.  It cannot widen what a collapse does; the
   order is tested again under the lock the collapse retakes.

For an anonymous table, and for a file table that gets collapsed, the lock
is given up and taken again at exactly the points it was before; the only
difference is that the caller is the one doing it.

DEBUG_VM config, in the five forms run_vmtests.sh runs it.  Every patch
builds, CONFIG_TRANSPARENT_HUGEPAGE=n included.

review_comments.raw_body:
From: "Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta)" <kas@kernel.org>

khugepaged.c holds both the users of collapse and the machinery that
performs it.  The daemon's scan loop, the sysfs tunables, MADV_COLLAPSE's
entry point and the collapse itself all sit in one file and reach into
each other freely.  Nothing marks where a user ends and the engine
begins.

Start drawing that line.

Add mm/collapse.h for what the two sides have to agree on:

  - enum scan_result - what the engine hands back;
  - struct collapse_control - the state a request carries.

And two constants move with them:

  - KHUGEPAGED_MAX_PTES_LIMIT -> COLLAPSE_MAX_PTES_LIMIT;
  - KHUGEPAGED_MIN_MTHP_ORDER -> COLLAPSE_MIN_MTHP_ORDER.

Neither is a fact about the daemon, so both lose the KHUGEPAGED_ prefix.

No functional change.

series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces the virtual swap device infrastructure, allowing for dynamic allocation of swap clusters and enabling the creation of a virtual swap device that can be used by vswap. The device is capped at approximately 8 TiB in size and uses a 64-bit architecture. It includes a dynamic cluster allocator and resolves swap entries' clusters under RCU. The patch also introduces a kernel parameter 'vswap=' to control the routing of vswap paths, defaulting to CONFIG_VSWAP_DEFAULT_ON. The device is not swappable or removable and can be used by vswap-aware paths in subsequent patches.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 02/11] mm, swap: support zswap and zero-filled swap pages as vswap backends
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds support for virtual swap (vswap) using zswap and zero-filled swap pages as backends, allowing compressed or zero-filled pages to be stored without pre-allocating physical swap space. It introduces a new vswap layer that decouples PTE swap entries from physical backing, enabling efficient compression and detection of zero-filled pages. The patch also includes changes to handle virtual swap-backed entries in the zswap shrinker and writeback paths, as well as updates to mem_cgroup_can_swap() to account for vswap's contribution to memory pressure. Additionally, it introduces a new function mem_cgroup_can_vswap() to determine whether vswap is enabled for a given cgroup.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 03/11] mm, swap: prepare the swap IO path for vswap
series_items.patch_summary: This patch prepares the swap IO path for vswap by allowing it to submit IO for a swap entry other than folio->swap. It achieves this by computing the sector from an explicit entry, which is then used in various functions such as swap_add_folio and __swap_writeout. This change enables the batching path to serve both vswap entries and physical entries mapped directly into PTEs. The patch also updates ops->can_merge to measure sectors and byte offsets from the batch head plus accumulated length instead of from the previous folio plus its size.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 04/11] mm, swap: support physical swap as a vswap backend
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds support for physical swap as a backend for the virtual swap layer, allowing zswap to allocate physical slots on demand when it declines a page. It introduces a new mechanism to track physical slots via pointer-tagged swap_table entries and modifies readahead and swapoff operations to work with this new system. The patch also includes changes to handle cases where zswap is disabled or the folio's cgroup does not support vswap, bypassing vswap and mapping the slot directly into PTEs.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 05/11] mm, swap: enable THP swapin for vswap entries
series_items.patch_summary: This patch enables transparent huge page (THP) swapin for vswap entries, allowing large anonymous folios to be swapped in as a unit when their vswap entries share contiguous physical swap slots on a synchronous IO device. This change improves performance by reducing the number of faults and retries required during swap operations. The patch also introduces checks for zswap-backed or mixed-backing batches, which are still refused and fall back to order-0 faults. The approach taken involves modifying existing functions in the mm module to handle vswap entries and THP swapin.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 06/11] mm, swap: write back vswap zswap entries to physical swap
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds support for writing back zswap-backed vswap entries to physical swap. It mirrors the existing zswap writeback path, but allocates the backing physical slot on demand at writeback time rather than pre-allocating it. The zswap shrinker no longer skips vswap entries unless there is no available physical swap space. The patch modifies the zswap_writeback_entry function to handle vswap entries by allocating physical backing before decompressing and storing the entry in the vtable.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 07/11] mm, swap: reclaim physical slots backing cache-only vswap entries
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses an issue where physical slots backing cache-only vswap entries are not being reclaimed when they become redundant. When a vswap entry's swap_count drops to 0 while its folio is still in the swap cache, the entry becomes cache-only and its physical slot is no longer needed. However, the current implementation does not properly reclaim these slots. This patch introduces a new flag, SWP_RMAP_CACHE_ONLY, to indicate when a vswap entry is cache-only, and modifies the physical reclaim scanner to reclaim such slots once swap usage exceeds 50%. The reclaimed slots are then freed, allowing for new allocations.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 08/11] mm, swap: only charge physical swap entries
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies how memory charge is handled for swap entries in Linux. It ensures that only physical swap entries are charged against a cgroup's swap, rather than all swap entries including zswap-backed and zero-filled pages. This change affects the behavior of memory.swap.current and allows cgroups to reclaim their anon memory even when memory.swap.max is set to 0. The patch also refactors the swap memcg operations into separate helpers for getting, recording, charging, uncharging, and putting swap entries.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 09/11] mm, swap: add debugfs counters for vswap
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds two debugfs counters to track virtual swap usage in the Linux kernel. The first counter, 'used', tracks the number of virtual swap slots (pages) currently allocated. The second counter, 'alloc_reject', counts the cumulative pages that failed to get a vswap slot. These counters are exposed under the '/sys/kernel/debug/vswap/' directory and can be accessed via debugfs. This patch addresses the need for visibility into virtual swap usage statistics, which is useful for debugging and performance analysis.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 10/11] mm, swap: defer memcg_table allocation for physical swap clusters
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes memory allocation for physical swap clusters by deferring the allocation of a memcg table until it is actually needed. This reduces unnecessary memory usage in cases where a cluster only holds vswap backings, which do not require a memcg table. The patch modifies the swap_cluster_alloc_table function to allocate the memcg table eagerly only when the cluster is known to be used for direct mapping or when vswap is disabled.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v5 11/11] mm, swap: back vswap clusters with a VM_SPARSE array
series_items.patch_summary: This patch replaces the vswap cluster's individually allocated memory with a VM_SPARSE array, simplifying access and reducing overhead. The new approach eliminates per-cluster allocation, xarray nodes, and RCU grace periods, making it more efficient. The swap_cluster_info_dynamic wrapper is removed, and the virtual table for a vswap cluster is freed when it empties, reclaiming most of its memory. This change aims to improve performance and reduce memory usage in the Linux kernel's swap management.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series introduces Virtual Swap Space (vswap), a feature that allows Linux to use a portion of physical memory as swap space, improving performance and reducing the need for disk-based swap. The patches address various issues and cleanups, including overcommit guessing, swapfile size limits, and memcg private id refcnt saturation. Additionally, they refactor swap-related operations into composable building blocks and introduce a new data structure to replace the xarray. The series also includes several bug fixes and performance improvements.

review_comments.author: Nhat Pham (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed a concern about the vswap device being capped at REFCOUNT_MAX pages, which can lead to memcg private id refcnt saturation when swapping past that limit. The author explained that this is not specific to vswap and also affects physical swapfiles of similar size, but acknowledged that it's an issue worth addressing.

review_comments.author: Nhat Pham (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed a concern about the OVERCOMMIT_GUESS heuristic, which gates allocations based on totalram_pages() + total_swap_pages. The author explained that vswap deliberately contributes to neither totalram_pages nor total_swap_pages, so when vswap is enabled, the bound collapses to RAM alone and allocations that vswap could absorb are refused. To fix this, the author added 2 * totalram_pages() to the OVERCOMMIT_GUESS heuristic when vswap and zswap are both on, for a 3x RAM ceiling plus whatever physical swap exists.

review_comments.author: Nhat Pham (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed a concern about the swap IO path being unable to submit IO for vswap entries backed by physical slots, which identify neither the backing device nor sector. The author modified the code to compute and store the sector from an explicit entry (swap_entry_sector), allowing batching to serve both vswap and physical entries.

review_comments.author: Nhat Pham (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed concerns about the swapoff path needing to drop the per-vswap spinlock before calling try_to_unmap(), explaining that dirtying would write uninitialized memory out to swap and instead a failed read leaves the folio not uptodate, so it's dropped. The loss is now reported as SIGBUS on the next fault rather than silently returning stale data.

review_comments.author: Nhat Pham (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed a concern about zswap-backed vswap entries being rejected due to lack of physical backing, explained that the backing is checked when the folio enters the swap cache and cannot change after that, and confirmed that the issue is resolved.

review_comments.author: Nhat Pham (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed a concern that zswap-backed and zero-filled pages were being charged against memcg->swap, which led to incorrect swap space usage tracking. The author agreed to change the charging behavior so that it occurs when a vswap entry acquires physical backing rather than at allocation. This will fix issues with memory.swap.current counting only on-disk swap usage, allow cgroups to reclaim their anon memory even if memory.swap.max is set to 0, and enable the charge to fail at writeback instead of at allocation.

Author disagreed with the claim of difficulty and suggested Baoquan should drive the switch if there are performance wins.

> fragmentation of the code path.

This will mirror my response at [1], but I'm responding here for the
record and for your convenience.

It is needed because vswap *is* a special device, with its own
requirements. If you don't special case-it, you'd get undesirable
behaviors.

Let's take Baoquan's patch series as an example.  It treats the xswap
device as just another swap device, without any special consideration
for it. Which creates several problem:

1. At allocation time, cgroups that disable zswap might get an xswap
slot, because you don't do any check that the device you allocating
the swap slots for is xswap. At swap_writeout() time, it is *stuck* -
we already do the unmapping step, so we cannot reclaim the page.

Ironically a physical swapfile backend could have bailed us out here,
but it's not in that patch series yet :)

Vswap both has swapfile backend, AND allows you to bypass it if the
cgroup disables zswap. Both involves a bit of swap_is_vswap() check,
but I think it's worth it :)

2. Per-CPU allocation caching: since all devices share the same cache,
xswap will invalidate the caching of other devices, and vice versa. It
would be fine if the these devices are interchangeable, but as noted
above, it's not, especially without physical swapfile as the backend
option. So you're forced to taken the slow path more often.

Vswap gets around this by adding its own per-cpu allocation caching,

So by being too lazy and not carefully distinguish the swap devices,
not only does xswap not work for the writeback use case, it cannot
even work in deployments where some workloads (cgroup) select zswap,
whereas others select disk swap. It can only work if you intend to
have a single class of device - either virtual/xswap or disk swap -
but not both.

Maybe instead of just grepping for swap_is_vswap() and throw your hand
at the complexity, read the code and try to understand why it's
necessary first, then propose simplifications if you have good ideas
in minds.

sizing aspect, which we are already discussing in another thread,

interface with only one correct answer - what's the point?

conforming to the status quo.

review_comments.author: Chris Li
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Chris Li expressed concerns that treating vswap as 'just another swap device' would lead to issues with internal and external allocations, and expose userspace to misconfiguration risks. > > have following actions.
>
> Registering vswap's operation as into swap_ops isn't too hard. I
> frankly don't see much wins to it for vswap itself, but it's not hard
> to do if you like it.

I am offering these as ways to move forward with vswap. There is
always the alternaive to use xswap instead.

>
> What I'm disagreeing is treating it as "just another swap device". The
> implementation shares a lot of swap device's machinery, so I have
> don't mind adopting it, but you can't treat it like a normal swap
> device, and expose it to userspace like one. You get issues with
> allocations internally, and externally you give userspace a vector to
> misconfigure with device priority.

I'd like to hear more about this. If a user wants to shoot themselves
in the foot. My philosophy is just let them. It is not worthwhile to
complicate the code path. We can add a big fat warning that
"Oh, you are configuring xswap with a priority other than the
recommended one." But if the user really wants to do it, we should
allow it.

Another use case is when users employ more than one swap device to
reduce swap device lock contention. It is not a big deal when you swap
out a few GB of memory. But if you swap out more than 100G of memory,
the swap device lock contention really shows up in the earlier version
of the swap core. The new swap allocator and swap table significantly
reduce that contention. But that contention still exists. A few
hundred G of memory under one lock is just a bit too much. I think
there is a legitimate reason to use more than one device to reduce
lock contention.

Granted, other ways exist to reduce lock contention, but they increase
code complexity as well. The current swap device design is a good
balance of code complexity and flexibility.

> That's why I've been insisting on what's the use case that motivates
> these aspects of the interface that you're interested in. A pretty
> design is not a real usecase, especially one that creates problems
> with userspace misconfigurations.

Points taken; this isn't enough to justify the extra maintenance and
complexity of vswap right now. A cleaner alternative exists with less
complexity overhead.

Chris

> Changelog:

> * v1 [v1] -> v2:
>     * Rebased to a newer mm-unstable tip.
>     * Fix a bunch of assorted issues (incorrect zswap store failure
>       rollback, vswap_init() failure handling, rmap-encoding collision,

>       more closely follow existing patterns, etc.).
>     * Some more code clean up and simplification: some renamings to more
>       closely follow existing patterns, move vswap backing check to
>       __swap_cache_add_check, store zero state in the swap_table for
>       vswap entries, etc.. Many of these are proposed by Kairui Song
>       in [1].
>     * Defer memcg_table allocation on physical clusters until the first
>       vswap-backing slot installs. Saves ~512 bytes per physical cluster
>       that only serves vswap-backing slots (this is the new patch 8).
>     * Widen swap_info_struct->max and ->pages (and the swapoff unuse-path
>       index) so vswap supports ~8 PB of swap space (this is the new
>       patch 9).
>     * Split the physical-swap-backend patch into three for reviewability:
>       the core backend (patch 3), zswap writeback to physical swap
>       (patch 4), and reclaim of cache-only physical slots (patch 5). No
>       functional change.
>     * Add kerneldoc for the vswap API.
>     * Add some benchmark numbers for zswap case.
> 
> 
> Patch 11 is an RFC. It swaps vswap's cluster xarray for the VM_SPARSE
> vmalloc array Baoquan He designed for xswap, to show that the data
> structure and the device model are separable: moving to his is one
> self-contained patch that adds no userspace interface. Note that
> per Baoquan's commentary (see [5]), I have skipped shrink for now, only
> freeing vtable when the cluster becomes free to minimize metadata
> overhead while keeping the skeleton in the free list. I have not done
> performance testing on this patch yet (the number is from the old design),
> but I have run a suite of simple stress tests.
> 
> It is adapted almost entirely from Baoquan's code (see [6]), so I have
> kept Baoquan's Co-developed-by and Signed-off-by tag.
> 
> 
> I. Context and Motivation
> =========================
> 
> Currently, when an anon page is swapped out, a slot in a backing swap
> device is allocated and stored in the page table entries that refer to
> the original page. This slot is also used as the "key" to find the
> swapped out content, as well as the index to swap data structures, such
> as the swap cache, or the swap cgroup mapping. Tying a swap entry to its
> backing slot in this way is performant and efficient when swap is purely
> just disk space, and swapoff is rare.
> 
> However, the advent of many swap optimizations has exposed major
> drawbacks of this design. The first problem is that we occupy a physical
> slot in the swap space, even for pages that are NEVER expected to hit
> the disk: pages compressed and stored in the zswap pool, zero-filled
> pages, or pages rejected by both of these optimizations when zswap
> writeback is disabled. This is arguably the central shortcoming of
> zswap:
> * Resource-wise, it is hugely wasteful in terms of disk usage. At Meta,
>   we size swapfile in the order of 25-50% of host RAM, depending on flash
>   availability. This is a lot of flash for a fleet of our size, and
>   with universal zswap enablement, most of this is wasted for zswap
>   entries.
> 
> * In deployments when no disk space can be afforded for swap (such as
>   mobile and embedded devices), users cannot adopt zswap, and are forced
>   to use zram. This is confusing for users, and creates extra burdens
>   for developers, having to develop and maintain similar features for
>   two separate swap backends (writeback, cgroup charging, THP support,
>   etc.). For instance, see the discussion in [2].
> 
> * Tying zswap (and more generally, other in-memory swap backends) to
>   the current physical swapfile infrastructure makes zswap implicitly
>   statically sized. This does not make sense, as unlike disk swap, in
>   which we consume a limited resource (disk space or swapfile space) to
>   save another resource (memory), zswap consumes the same resource it is
>   saving (memory). The more we zswap, the more memory we have available,
>   not less. We are not rationing a limited resource when we limit
>   the size of the zswap pool, but rather we are capping the resource
>   (memory) saving potential of zswap. Under memory pressure, using
>   more zswap is almost always better than the alternative (disk IOs, or
>   even worse, OOMs), and dynamically sizing the zswap pool on demand
>   allows the system to flexibly respond to these precarious scenarios.
> 
> * Operationally, static provisioning the swapfile for zswap poses
>   significant challenges, because the sysadmin has to prescribe how
>   much swap is needed a priori, for each combination of
>   (memory size x disk space x workload usage). It is even more
>   complicated when we take into account the variance of memory
>   compression, which changes the reclaim dynamics (and as a result,
>   swap space size requirement). The problem is further exacerbated for
>   users who rely on swap utilization (and exhaustion) as an OOM signal.
> 
>   All of these factors make it very difficult to configure the swapfile
>   for zswap: too small of a swapfile and we risk preventable OOMs and
>   limit the memory saving potentials of zswap; too big of a swapfile
>   and we waste disk space and memory due to swap metadata overhead.
>   This dilemma becomes more drastic in high memory systems, which can
>   have up to TBs worth of memory.
> 
> Swap virtualization is the answer to these issues, with three properties:
> 
> 1. Decoupled backends. For zswap in particular, this means we eliminate
>    the unused storage space, and allows zswap to be used in systems that
>    do not have enough storage capacity for physical swap (without having
>    to resort to silly hacks). Zero-filled swap pages and swap-cache-only
>    folios also benefit here.
> 
> 2. Dynamic swap space. Since virtual swap is not tied to any physical
>    resource, we can make it effectively infinite and dynamically grow it
>    on demand.
>    This massively simplifies operational provisioning, and increases the
>    utilization of compressed swap backends (zswap). Dynamicity also
>    reduces overhead on unused swap capacity.
> 
> 3. Efficient backend transfer. The virtualization scheme should not
>    introduce PTE/rmap walking overhead for backend transfer. This
>    is crucial for systems that want to support multiple swap backends
>    in a tiering fashion (for e.g zswap -> disk swap).
> 
> For more historical contexts and references, please take a look at
> the cover letter of the older vswap submissions ([3] and [v2]).
> 
> II. Design
> ==========
> 
> When vswap is enabled (via vswap=on cmdline parameter), a special vswap
> device is allocated at boot time. Anon pages that can be zswapped will
> obtain a vswap slot at swap allocation time.
> 
> These swap entries can subsequently acquire backend on-demand, such as
> a zswap entry, or a slot on a physical swap device (as a fallback option
> or at zswap writeback time).
> 
> We repurpose much of the existing swap_table infrastructure and
> swapfile allocator for this new vswap device, with two notable
> differences:
> * Clusters are dynamically allocated on demand and managed through
>   an xarray. This in turn allows us to avoid static provisioning and
>   let swap space grow dynamically.
> 
> * Each cluster of this new vswap device has a virtual_table that stores
>   the backend information of the entries in the cluster (see below).
> 
> Diagrams:
> 
>   Case 1: vswap entry (virtualized)
> 
>   PTE                  swap_cluster_info_dynamic
>   vswap_entry          +---------------------------------+
>   (swp_entry_t) ------>| swap_cluster_info (ci)          |
>                        | +----------------------------+  |
>                        | | swap_table                 |  |
>                        | |   PFN / Shadow             |  |
>                        | | memcg_table                |  |
>                        | | count,flags,order          |  |
>                        | | lock, list                 |  |
>                        | +----------------------------+  |
>                        |                                 |
>                        | virtual_table                   |
>                        | +----------------------------+  |
>                        | | NONE                       |  |
>                        | | SWAPFILE(swp_entry_t)      |  |
>                        | | ZSWAP(struct zswap_entry*) |  |
>                        | +----------------------------+  |
>                        +---------------------------------+
>                               |
>                               | SWAPFILE resolves to
>                               v
>                        PHYSICAL CLUSTER (swap_cluster_info)
>                        +--------------------------+
>                        | swap_table per-slot:     |
>                        |   NULL   - free          |
>                        |   PFN    - cached folio  |
>                        |   Shadow - swapped out   |
>                        |   Pointer- vswap rmap    |
>                        |   Bad    - unusable      |
>                        |                          |
>                        | Vswap-backing slot:      |
>                        |   Pointer(C|swp_entry_t) |
>                        |     rmap back to vswap   |
>                        +--------------------------+
> 
>   Case 2: direct-mapped physical entry (no vswap)
> 
>   PTE                  PHYSICAL CLUSTER (swap_cluster_info)
>   phys_entry           +--------------------------+
>   (swp_entry_t) ------>| swap_table per-slot:     |
>                        |   NULL   - free          |
>                        |   PFN    - cached folio  |
>                        |   Shadow - swapped out   |
>                        |   Bad    - unusable      |
>                        +--------------------------+
> 
> struct swap_cluster_info_dynamic {
>     struct swap_cluster_info ci;       /* swap_table, lock, etc. */
>     unsigned int index;                /* position in xarray */
>     struct rcu_head rcu;               /* kfree_rcu deferred free */
>     atomic_long_t *virtual_table;      /* backend info, 8 B/slot */
> };
> 
> Each vswap cluster (swap_cluster_info_dynamic) extends the classic
> swap_cluster_info struct with a virtual_table array that stores the
> backend information for each virtual swap entry in the cluster. Each
> entry is tag-encoded in the low 3 bits to indicate the backend type:
> 
>   NONE:     |----- 0000 ------|000|  free / unbacked
>   ZSWAP:    |--- zswap_entry* |001|  compressed in zswap
>   SWAPFILE: |- type:5,off:56 -|010|  on a physical swapfile
> 
> Other design highlights:
> 
> * Note that for the vswap device, we have merged the zswap xarray tree
>   with the swapfile-level clusters. This means that for zswap only users,
>   we have negligible extra space overhead.
> 
> * Both vswap entries (Case 1) and directly-mapped physical entries
>   (Case 2) coexist as first-class citizens.
> 
> * Backend transitions in the virtual_table are synchronized through the
>   swap cache and the folio lock - the same mechanism that already
>   serializes ordinary swap operations (swapin, swapout, zswap
>   writeback, swap cache reclaim). IOW, we can only assume that the
>   backend of a vswap entry is stable through swap cache/folio lock.
>   Looking at the backend without this should be done at best for
>   optimization purposes, as there is no guarantee that the backend
>   will not change under the observer.
> 
> * Pointer-tagged swap_table entries on physical clusters provide the
>   rmap (physical -> virtual) lookup.
> 
> * Virtual swap slots not backed by physical swap are not charged to
>   memcg swap counters - only physical backing is charged (I made the
>   case for this in [4]).
> 
> III. Benchmarks
> ===============
> 
> Note that the goal is not to match vswap performance with baseline on
> every single case yet - running with vswap off is still supported. We
> can optimize further once we have landed this new feature.
> 
> A. Production Workload: Instagram
> =================================
> 
> To test vswap's stability and performance, I ran an A/B experiment on
> Instagram (django) workload, with zswap as the swap backend. On these
> hosts, the swapfiles' size is 50% of RAM.
> 
> Compared to baseline, vswap gives:
> 
> * On par request throughput.
> * Lower request serving latency (by about 1-3%).
> * Lower memory pressure in the system service cgroups running alongside
>   the workload. PSI-based proactive reclaimer can therefore recover more
>   from them, lowering their overall memory footprint, allowing the main
>   workload to expand.
> * Elimination of swapfile footprint for all zswap users in the host.
> 
> B. Semi-synthetic Workloads (memhog, usemem, kernel build)
> ==========================================================
> 
> All values are mean +/- standard deviation across rounds.
> 
> Test system: x86_64, 52 cores, 64 GB swapfile for all 3 benchmarks.
> Swap backend: zswap (zstd) with the traditional active/inactive LRU. We
> focus on zswap here because it is the motivating use case for vswap.
> 
> For each benchmark, we test 3 kernels:
> * Baseline: mm-unstable, no vswap patches.
> * VSS off: vswap series applied, vswap=off, to verify that there is no
>   regression to existing swap paths when we disable vswap.
> * VSS on: vswap series applied, vswap=on.
> 
> 1. Memhog: single-threaded, 48GB allocation on a host with 16GB RAM,
>    20 rounds.
> 
>                     Baseline           VSS off            VSS on
>    real (s)        124.05 +/- 11.64   122.31 +/- 10.29   118.57 +/- 15.68
>    sys (s)         106.75 +/- 10.86   105.01 +/- 9.64    101.34 +/- 13.97
>    user (s)        10.81 +/- 0.11     10.85 +/- 0.09     10.79 +/- 0.09
>    delta real              -              -1.4%              -4.4%
>    delta sys               -              -1.6%              -5.1%
> 
> Dropping the best and the worst round to reduce variance:
> 
>    memhog              Baseline           VSS off            VSS on

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 1/7] cgroup: add cgroup_account_system_time()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new helper function, cgroup_account_system_time(), which charges kernel CPU time to a cgroup's cpu.stat. The function is designed to be used in conjunction with the next patch, where it will be utilized for kernel threads working on behalf of other cgroups.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 2/7] cgroup: add set_active_cgroup() to charge CPU time to a cgroup
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new function called set_active_cgroup() that allows a kernel thread to charge its CPU time to a specific cgroup instead of its own cgroup, usually root. The function sets the task's active_cgroup field and returns the old value. It first charges the time used so far to the old cgroup before setting the new active cgroup. This is necessary for tasks like memcg reclaim from a workqueue that do work for a cgroup but are not part of it. Only kernel threads in the root cgroup can call this function, and it warns and does nothing if called by other processes. The patch also adds code to charge system time to the active cgroup when set under set_active_cgroup().

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 3/7] psi: charge pressure to the task's active cgroup
series_items.patch_summary: This patch updates the Pressure Stall Information (PSI) system to charge pressure to a task's active control group when it stalls, such as during memory reclaim. The active cgroup is determined by the set_active_cgroup function and updated accordingly. When the active cgroup changes, the task's pressure state is moved from the old groups to the new ones, similar to how real cgroup moves are handled. This change ensures that PSI accurately reflects the pressure on a task's current control group.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 4/7] sched/fair: add cfs_bandwidth_charge() for kernel work done for a cgroup
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new function, cfs_bandwidth_charge(), which charges kernel work done by a task to its controlling cgroup's CPU time budget. The function takes into account the cgroup's own quota and that of its ancestors with limits, ensuring that the work does not starve the group for long. If the pool cannot cover the work, it becomes debt, paid out of subsequent refills. This change is necessary to accurately reflect kernel work done by a task in the cgroup's CPU time usage statistics.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 5/7] cgroup: take set_active_cgroup() time out of the cgroup's cpu.max
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the set_active_cgroup() function to charge kernel time used by tasks to their current cgroup's cpu.max quota, in addition to updating the task's active cgroup. This ensures that CPU usage is accurately accounted for and reflected in the cgroup's statistics. The change involves storing the task's runtime at each set_active_cgroup() call and then charging the old cgroup with the used time when the active cgroup changes.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 6/7] memcg: charge high_work reclaim to the memcg
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the behavior of high_work reclaim in the Linux kernel's memory cgroup (memcg) subsystem. When a memcg exceeds its memory.high limit, the reclaim process is currently run from a kworker thread in the root cgroup, which means it doesn't get charged to the memcg's cpu.stat or memory.pressure metrics and doesn't count against its cpu.max quota. This patch changes the reclaim process to run under set_active_cgroup(), which charges its CPU time and memory stalls to the memcg's cgroup and deducts from its cpu.max quota, providing a more accurate representation of the memcg's resource usage.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 7/7] selftests: cgroup: check that high_work reclaim is charged to the memcg
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds two selftests to the Linux kernel's cgroup testing framework. The first test, `test_memcg_high_work`, checks that high-work reclaim is charged to the memory control group (memcg) by filling its TCP receive buffers from a softirq while only one task sleeps, causing the memcg to exceed its memory limit and triggering high-work reclaim. The second test, `test_memcg_high_work_cpu_max`, runs a CPU hog in the memcg under a cpu.max limit, ensuring that the hog gets less CPU time when high-work is busy. Both tests require swap space to be enabled so that anon memory can be reclaimed.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series introduces a mechanism to charge kernel work to the cgroup it is being done for, rather than charging it to the root cgroup. This addresses a problem where CPU time spent by kernel threads on behalf of a specific cgroup is not accounted for in that cgroup's statistics and quotas. The approach taken involves allowing kernel threads to specify which cgroup they are working for, and then updating the relevant statistics and quotas accordingly. This will improve resource isolation and accuracy of accounting for CPU usage in various scenarios, including memory reclaim from high-work queues.

review_comments.author: Tejun Heo
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Tejun Heo noted that the current approach of moving a kworker into the target cgroup before running it has scalability issues due to contention on cgroup_mutex and cgroup_threadgroup_rwsem, and suggested an alternative direction for remote charging where a kthread explicitly specifies which cgroup the work is intended for.

Reviewer noted that the proposed solution does not address net rx, another major source of displaced CPU usage, and suggested adopting an approach that can cover both memory reclaim and net rx use cases by counting per-cgroup received packets and prorating CPU consumption.

Reviewer Tejun Heo expressed concern about the unconditional forgiveness of debt capping, suggesting instead that the cgroup should be slowed down to throttle new work generation and avoid out-of-control situations, similar to IO control mechanisms.
review_comments.raw_body:
Hello, Shakeel.

On Thu, Sep 24, 2026 at 11:47:04AM -0700, Shakeel Butt wrote:

---

This doesn't translate to net rx, which is another major source of
displaced CPU usage. Switching membership on each packet isn't going to
work there. Attribution can't happen that way. We'd much rather count
per-cgroup received packets and prorate the CPU consumption. If at all
possible, I think it'd be better to adopt an approach which can cover
both use cases.

---

I don't like the debt capping. Having debt doesn't have to mean that
the cgroup doesn't get any bandwidth at all. The cgroup just needs to
be slowed down enough that the generation of new work is throttled and
the whole thing doesn't go out of control. IO control already does
this: when IO debt is accumulated, userspace is heavily throttled, but
not completely stalled, until the whole cgroup's consumption comes
under control. I don't see why the debts would need to be forgiven
unconditionally. The cgroup can keep paying them while running at a
minimal rate to avoid triggering stall failures, and if the situation
doesn't resolve quickly, that will most likely trigger pressure based
kills in any reasonable setup anyway.

Thanks.

--
tejun

review_comments.author: Shakeel Butt (author)
review_comments.summary:
Author acknowledged a concern about accurate accounting of CPU time spent on network receive operations, particularly for modern NICs with dedicated rx queues and old NICs with shared queues. They proposed extending the mechanism to softirqs and considering a special way to account for the latter case, possibly through BPF.

Author agreed to address a concern about CPU time capping and promised to restructure it in the next patch version.
review_comments.raw_body:
Very good point. I think we need to think for net rx for two scenarios. First,
the modern NICs with rx steering support and second, old NIC with shared queues.

On the modern NICs where the workloads get their own rx queues, I think the
proposed mechanism can help to do the accurate accounting (I have to extend this
to softirqs as it is limited to kthreads atm) very easily.

The challenge you mentioned is for the old NICs where we get to know the cgroup
assosiation of the rx packets very late (or deep) in the stack. Also CPU spent
on each packet is not necessarily uniform (due to out-of-order or drops or
checksum errors or window shrinking) but for simplicity we can assume uniform
CPU. Maybe the right place to charge for such scenario might be at application
receiving those packets into the memory. I feel like we might need a very
special way to account for this case (maybe through BPF or something). At
the moment to me it seems very hard to have a universal solution which helps
this case and the reclaim case I am targetted.

If you don't mind, I think having solution for modern NICs i.e. dedicated rx
queues, should suffice for now (unless you want the solution for old NICs as
well). Let me know what you think.

---

Sounds good, I will remove this capping in the next version.

Thanks for taking a look.

review_comments.author: Tejun Heo
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Tejun Heo noted that the current approach to charging kernel work to a cgroup does not account for CPU time spent in common code for a specific cgroup, and requested remote charging of CPU time similar to IO and memory allocation.

Reviewer Tejun Heo expressed concerns that Rx steering is not suitable for attributing CPU cycles to each cgroup, citing its cumbersome setup and mismatched granularity.

Reviewer suggested combining net rx charging and reclaim CPU charging into a single mechanism where cycles are force-charged to the cgroup after the fact, without involving PSI.
review_comments.raw_body:
Hello, Shakeel.

On Thu, Sep 24, 2026 at 02:11:00PM -0700, Shakeel Butt wrote:

---

Rx steering is useful for partitioning the whole machine, but it doesn't
seem like the right tool for attributing CPU cycles to each cgroup. It's
cumbersome to set up and the granularity doesn't match. We aren't going
to be steering net rx processing per cgroup.

---

This doesn't have to be exact or completely synchronous. I don't see why
net rx charging and reclaim CPU charging can't share the same mechanism,
where the cycles are force charged to the cgroup after the fact.

I don't think PSI needs to be involved either. Shared execution in
itself shouldn't create pressure. The forced charge changes the cgroup's
usage, and that usage then creates pressure in the cgroup. IO works the
same way.

Thanks.

--
tejun

series_items.subject: [PATCH RESEND 1/7] locking: add opt-in tracking of sleeping lock holders
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces an opt-in tracking system for sleeping lock holders in the Linux kernel. It allows tasks to count and report the number of locks they hold that have opted into this tracking, enabling a cheap way to check if a task is holding a lock that other tasks may be waiting for. This feature can help avoid stalls caused by memory allocation while holding shared locks, such as cgroup_mutex or kernfs_rwsem. The patch adds new APIs and infrastructure to support this feature, including a new header file and kernel configuration options.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RESEND 2/7] locking/rwsem: track holders of opted-in rw_semaphores
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a feature to track the holders of read-write semaphores (rw_semaphores) in Linux. It introduces a new flag, `tracked`, which is set when an rw_semaphore is opted-in for holder tracking. The count of holders is incremented when a task acquires the lock and decremented when it releases the lock. This feature is designed to help with debugging and troubleshooting by providing information about who holds a particular lock. It also includes support for PREEMPT_RT builds, which have a different locking mechanism. The patch modifies several kernel files to implement this new feature.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RESEND 3/7] locking/mutex: track holders of opted-in mutexes
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a feature to track the holders of opted-in mutexes in Linux. It adds a function called `mutex_track_holder` that allows developers to opt-in mutexes for holder tracking. The function is used to count the number of locks held by a task, which can help identify potential bottlenecks and stalls in the system. The patch also includes changes to handle PREEMPT_RT builds and ensures that the tracking flag survives even after the lock has been released. The feature is opt-in, meaning it only applies to mutexes that have explicitly opted-in for holder tracking.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RESEND 4/7] locking/percpu-rwsem: track holders of opted-in percpu_rw_semaphores
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a feature to track the holders of percpu_rw_semaphores, which are used in various Linux kernel components such as filesystem freeze and async writes. The patch introduces a new function `percpu_rwsem_track_holder()` that allows opting-in percpu_rw_semaphores for holder tracking. It also updates several functions to count the lock holders correctly, ensuring that tasks are not preemptible while holding the lock without being counted. This feature is enabled by CONFIG_TRACK_LOCK_HOLDERS and adds a new field `tracked` to the percpu_rw_semaphore structure.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RESEND 5/7] locking/selftests: add KUnit tests for lock holder tracking
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds 16 KUnit tests to verify the lock holder tracking functionality in Linux. The tests cover various scenarios, including locks that did not opt-in, mutex and rw_semaphore calls, downgrade_write(), cleanup.h guards, nested locks released out of order, and percpu_rwsem_release()/percpu_rwsem_acquire() hand-off. Five tests use a helper thread to hold a lock and check the count, while three cases cover what the opt-in changes besides the count. The tests are designed to ensure that task_nr_tracked_locks(current) always equals the number of opted-in locks held by the task.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RESEND 6/7] Documentation/locking: document sleeping lock holder tracking
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds documentation to the Linux kernel's locking subsystem, specifically about sleeping lock holder tracking. The feature allows kernel code to identify tasks that are holding widely shared locks and may be causing stalls in other tasks waiting for those locks. It provides information on how a task can opt-in to being tracked, how the count is updated, and what it costs in terms of performance. The documentation also explains where each lock type updates the count and notes what is not covered by this feature.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RESEND 7/7] kernfs, cgroup: track holders of the cgroupfs locks
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the cgroupfs kernfs rwsems, cgroup_mutex and cgroup_threadgroup_rwsem by enabling lock holder tracking. This is done to prevent a stalled lock holder from stalling unrelated work in the cgroupfs control plane. The patch adds a new flag KERNFS_ROOT_TRACK_LOCK_HOLDERS that enables this feature for roots whose locks are shared widely across different operations, such as create, destroy and migrate. The patch also includes opt-ins for statically defined locks cgroup_mutex and cgroup_threadgroup_rwsem. This is part of a policy to read the count of lock holders, which should be implemented separately.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series introduces a mechanism to track sleeping lock holders in the Linux kernel. It allows locks to opt-in to being tracked, and stores a count of these locks in task_struct. This is intended to help solve isolation failures caused by shared locks, where one workload's pressure can leak into another unrelated workload. The solution aims to improve performance by allowing the allocator to treat tasks holding widely shared locks differently, especially under memory or CPU pressure.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 2/4] memcg_ext: add cgroup-attached bpf_memcg_ops
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds an empty bpf_memcg_ops type to allow attaching memory policies to cgroups, which is the first step in making memcg enforcement programmable one hook at a time. The patch also moves cgroup BPF attach types outside of CONFIG_CGROUP_BPF and fixes struct_ops registration stubs for all supported configurations. This does not change any existing behavior yet.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 3/4] memcg_ext: allow BPF to defer memory.high enforcement
series_items.patch_summary: This patch allows BPF (Berkeley Packet Filter) programs to defer memory.high enforcement, which prevents tasks holding kernel locks from being stuck in the charge path. It introduces high_policy ops that provide a read-only snapshot of the charge and allow programs to return a request. This approach enables more efficient handling of memory allocation and deallocation by allowing BPF programs to skip inline calls and re-entering the charge path.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 4/4] selftests/bpf: add a cgroupfs lock-holder bpf_memcg_ops sample
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a BPF (Berkeley Packet Filter) sample to track and enforce policies on tasks holding cgroupfs kernfs locks. The policy, called bpf_memcg_ops, prevents tasks from being inline memory.high enforced if they hold such locks. It does this by tracking the depth of kernfs_rwsem and kernfs_supers_rwsem locks per task using fentry/fexit hooks. Two counters are used to guard against incorrect enforcement. The patch is measured to improve performance on a reproducer, reducing stall times and increasing throughput.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series, memcg_ext, introduces a new struct_ops type called bpf_memcg_ops to attach memory controller policy to a cgroup through a cgroup-attached struct_ops. The goal is to prevent tasks from being stuck while holding kernel locks due to memory reclaim and throttling. A specific problem addressed by this patch is the kernfs notify worker, which can be stuck while holding the cgroup2 kernfs_rwsem lock. The patch adds a new policy called high_policy that allows policies to specify where memory.high should be enforced instead of inlining the call. Measurements show significant improvements in performance and latency compared to the baseline and an existing fix for a similar problem.

review_comments.summary: Reviewer suggested that the policy should notify userspace via ringbuf when it defers debt, and proposed a userspace reclaimer to handle the reclaim through memory.reclaim; they also proposed using clone3(CLONE_INTO_CGROUP) to charge CPU usage of the spawned reclaimer to the target cgroup
review_comments.raw_body:
Hello Shakeel,

On the open question of how deferred debt eventually gets paid: would
it make sense for the policy to also notify userspace (e.g. via
ringbuf) when it defers, and have a userspace reclaimer do the reclaim
through memory.reclaim?

I understand one of the concerns for the async worker is CPU
accounting. If the concern is that the kworker's CPU usage is not
charged to the target cgroup, the userspace reclaimer could instead be
spawned with clone3(CLONE_INTO_CGROUP) so it runs inside the target
cgroup, and both its CPU and memory usage get charged there.

One caveat: intermediate cgroups with the no-internal-process
constraint cannot take processes, so this would only work for leaf
cgroups.

What do you think?

Sure. On our production servers we have been running a set of BPF
programs to tailor kernel behavior for different workloads — all of
them global programs so far — and I believe they are all good
candidates for per-cgroup BPF policies now that cgroup-attached
struct_ops is available. They have been really helpful in our
Kubernetes production environment. I have sent some of them upstream,
such as:

  - BPF-THP
    https://lwn.net/Articles/1039689/
  - BPF-auto-NUMA
    https://lwn.net/Articles/1054030/

Perhaps we can revisit both of them and turn them into per-cgroup
policies — what do you think?

We are also running some custom BPF programs that have not been sent
upstream yet, such as:

  - BPF-async-reclaimer
    We don't care about the CPU accounting of the kworker, so we just
wake up a kworker to do the async reclaiming.
  - BPF-fault-around

Both are really beneficial to our workloads, and both are global programs today.

We are planning a few more customizations to resolve painful
production issues, such as:

  - The long-standing inode::lock contention caused by dentries [0].
    We have not started implementing it yet, but we might introduce a
memcg->dentry_limit or a memcg->vfs_cache_pressure as BPF policies..
  - cgroup-level readahead.

So, to answer your question directly: for memcg itself, the beneficial
customizations for us are the reclaim policy (the async reclaimer
above), the dentry/vfs cache pressure knobs, and fault-around; the
rest are per-cgroup MM policies that would need the
struct_ops-to-cgroup mechanism generalized beyond memcg — which is why
I hope these use cases can help make the design more generic.

[0] https://lore.kernel.org/linux-fsdevel/20240511200240.6354-2-torvalds@linux-foundation.org/

-- 
Regards
Yafang

review_comments.raw_body:

On Mon, Sep 21, 2026 at 12:25:55PM -0700, Shakeel Butt wrote:

---

Why not just raise the lazy bound high enough that most charges never
enforce inline, and maybe annotate the specific paths that can allocate a
lot so that they do? Inline enforcement should be the exception, not the
rule. Flipping that and then trying to reverse it with custom BPF policies
doesn't make a lot of sense.

---

Slowing down the kworker inline doesn't make sense. It's charging on behalf
of the watcher through set_active_memcg(), which already tells us whose debt
it is. Wouldn't it make more sense to defer the debt to that cgroup instead
of slowing down the kernel thread?
